messages.subject: Regression: removing predictors increases sampling time
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to solve a regression problem using a log-normal distribution whose location and scale both depend polynomially on the predictor, however when I reduce the degree of the scale's polynomial, the sampling time increases (even though the model gets simpler).

Here's a model that captures what I'm trying to do:

data {
    int<lower=1> C;                   // dimension (degree) location regressors.
    int<lower=1> D;                   // dimension of scale regressors.
    int<lower=1> N;                   // number of data points.
    matrix[N, C] L;                     // location regressors.
    matrix<lower=0>[N, D] S;    // scale regressors.
    vector<lower=0>[N] Y;         // outcomes.
}
parameters {
    vector[C] alpha;
    vector<lower=0>[D] beta;
}
model {
    Y ~ lognormal(L * alpha, S * beta);
  
    alpha ~ normal(0, 1);
    beta   ~ normal(0, 1);
}

And here are the results of some timed runs on my data:

C = 4, D = 2:
1 loop, best of 3: 32.9 s per loop

C = 4, D = 3:
1 loop, best of 3: 24 s per loop

C = 4, D = 4:
1 loop, best of 3: 12.6 s per loop

In this case N was 500 (but the issue showed up on my full dataset of about 9000 points); I initialised using fixed values; and all three inferences pretty much agree. I've applied this model to random data and the issue didn't really seem to show up, so I think it's data-specific.

I'm trying to figure out — and I'd be grateful if someone could provide an explanation — why the simpler model can take longer to sample. I've re-implemented the model in quite a few ways, but the issue remains. At this point I think it has to do with what Bob Carpenter mentioned in this answer, regarding the automatic differentiation that's happening behind the scenes, but I'd like some clarity so I know how to handle these situations in the future.

A few quick notes:
  • I wanted the model to be able to handle non-polynomial regression too, and allow for separate location and scale regressors.
  • Generally my values are binned, so there are quite a few duplicates — I've done some experiments and found that the sampler performs much faster if I use a ragged data structure rather than the flat one I've shown above. It might be worth mentioning this in the section on flat/ragged data structures (Chapter 15 in 2.14) in the manual? (Since in this case the vectorised implementation is in fact slower.)
  • In the end I'm probably going to set C = D and use all the regressors for both parameters anyway, because I'm not trying to do model comparison; however, this is bugging me.
Thanks,
Kevin

parts:
Model (mis)specification affects time. So if the lower-order
thing doesn't fit as well (for example, there may be a lot of uncertainty),
it can slow things down. You might want to check the scales of
your priors.

The log density and gradient will be faster for the simpler model,
but it may take leapfrog steps will be faster, but it may take more leapfrog
steps per iteration.

And don't forget it's all probabilistic, so you have to look
at multiple runs to get a trend.

- Bob

To Bob: I understand that when the simpler model doesn't explain the data well the posterior might be more difficult to sample from, but in this case the simple model seems to do a pretty good job: when a quadratic or cubic term is added to the scale's polynomial, the inferred coefficients are essentially zero. To Andrew: My application is distance vs time — from a plot, it seems like there's a linear trend for large distances, but this isn't the case for small distances, where there seems to be a bit of curvature. If polynomial regression is a bad idea in this case, my issue could very well just be a resulting anomaly. Regarding the scale of the coefficients, in this case the only parameters that aren't on the unit scale are those unique to the complex model.

I'm not hugely concerned about all this though — it clearly has to do with a combination of my data and model, and I've already got a decent answer. I guess my confusion is just the following: the complex model seems to fit the data nicely (and samples quickly), but it isn't 'using' the parameters it has over-and-above the simpler model, so I would think that the simpler model is good enough, and therefore should sample just as quickly.
